A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CODE2BENCH and retain its Scope Graph/PBT framework. The complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables, equations, and examples, support comparison despite the changed title and benchmark release.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 16 LLMs, including multilingual Pass@1 results, failure distributions, difficulty analyses, and near-perfect failure rates in Section 4 and Appendix I.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of 10 LLMs on Python and Java tracks, judge-agreement studies in Appendix D, and a numerical-failure case study in Appendix J.

M1.justification: The central dependency-analysis, semantic-filtering, and PBT pipeline remains; the 100% coverage gate already existed. v2 reports native Java construction, adds optional greedy test-suite minimization in Appendix I.1, and sketches recursive dependency bundling and completion-task generation in Appendix K. The latter are proposed extensions, not demonstrated replacements for the core pipeline.

E1.justification: The five-language evaluation of Python-derived SC tasks is replaced by native SC-Python, WSC-Python, and SC-Java tracks, including tasks sourced from Java repositories. JavaScript, TypeScript, and Go evaluation disappears. Layered dependency and code-completion tasks remain future proposals rather than evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated model roster changes substantially from 16 to 10. Claude-4-Sonnet replaces Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Gemma-3n-e4b-it appears, and models including Doubao, Llama-4-Maverick, and both Qwen2.5-Coder variants disappear. The direct EvalPlus/HumanEval benchmark comparison remains.

E3.justification: The reported source window changes from August 2024–May 2025 to May–September 2025. v1 evaluates 193 shared SC tasks across five languages plus 198 WSC tasks; v2 uses 217 SC-Python, 194 WSC-Python, and 249 native SC-Java tasks. Shared-task cross-language testing gives way to separate native collections. New judge-validation studies use samples of 100 and 50 functions; zero-shot greedy Pass@1 remains.

E4.justification: v2 replaces the three-category failure analysis with finer diagnostic distributions covering syntax, runtime, logical, and partial-success outcomes. It adds inter-LLM/human filtering validation in Appendix D and a detailed numerical-error case study in Appendix J. The difficulty-stratified performance analyses from v1 Section 4.6 and Appendix I.3 are removed, although difficulty-labeling prompts remain.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without uncertainty intervals. v2 Table 3 adds 95% confidence intervals throughout, while Appendix D introduces Fleiss’ kappa and Cohen’s kappa agreement analyses. The PDFs do not specify how the confidence intervals were constructed or establish additional repeated model runs.

E6.justification: The benchmark results are substantially replaced. DeepSeek-V3 scores 39.3%/50.5%/25.9% on v1 SC-Python/WSC-Python/translated Java, versus 34.4%/37.6%/47.8% on v2 SC-Python/WSC-Python/native Java (v1 Tables 2–3; v2 Table 3). These are different task collections, not same-setting performance changes. v2 also adds agreement coefficients and case-study findings, while removing difficulty-specific results.

T1.justification: Appendix K.1 adds a recursive definition of Layered Self-Contained functions whose internal dependencies resolve to SC/WSC functions. The existing Scope Graph formalism, SC/WSC classification rules, and cyclomatic-complexity formula in Appendices B–C remain unchanged. No new theorem or formal proof is supplied.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion recast the contribution around Dual Scaling, native Python/Java benchmarks, and diagnostic fingerprints. The earlier emphasis on cross-language transfer weaknesses is replaced by claims about language-dependent failure patterns, including a new claim to first systematically quantify language-ecosystem effects.

C2.justification: v2 hypothesizes that Java’s static typing provides performance scaffolding and interprets numerical near-misses as engineering-robustness failures. It strengthens the generalization-versus-memorization interpretation and adds specific limitations concerning discarded defensive branches and excluded reasoning models. The existing functional-correctness limitations are retained, moving from Appendix J to L.

D1.justification: v2 adds repository-selection and stratified-sampling details, construction-funnel counts, a native Java Javadoc prompt, and construction-cost estimates. It removes v1’s validity/portability subsection and several multilingual prompts and worked examples. Documentation remains inconsistent: Appendix F still describes Python-to-Java translation, and Appendix I.1 retains the old 16-model/1,163-task accounting.

R1.justification: Most related-work comparisons remain intact. v2 adds references and discussion involving AutoCodeBench, DomainEval, QuickCheck, McCabe’s complexity measure, and syntax-aware completion, while dropping several background/model citations. These are limited literature updates rather than a wholesale replacement of the research context.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, framework exposition, evaluation narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around Dual Scaling and diagnostics. Evaluation subsections are consolidated and reordered, while appendix organization changes substantially, including relocation of evaluation prompts and limitations.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned; v2 adds the benchmark-landscape visualization and replaces the aggregate failure bars with diagnostic ridgelines. Performance tables are reorganized into native tracks with confidence intervals, and new benchmark-characteristics and construction-funnel tables appear. Appendix listings and conference-page formatting also change.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful filter validation, uncertainty reporting, and native Java evidence. However, its stronger language-effect interpretation uses different task collections instead of v1’s matched tasks, and Table 3 contradicts a uniform WSC advantage for the two closed-source models. Stale Java-generation instructions and old compute accounting further weaken reproducibility. These substantive gains and unresolved validity problems prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
